As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. A number of contemporary studies have attempted to bring more theoretical precision to the concept of ambience, many doing so by resuscitating the more active, embracing connotations of the Greek periechon. These contemporary attempts characteristically emphasize ambience's role in perception, as when Jean-Paul Thibaud says that "ambience puts us in immediate contact with a situation in its entirety" (2). Such an approach rejects the notion of situations as mere composites of what is subjectively requisite, or the intersection of networking strands, with everything else relegated to epiphenomena, and instead sees a11 elements as operational and even necessary, albeit at various levels of scale. But not all these elements are oriented on the perceiving subject, making ambience transubjective, hence the necessity for an ecological conception of the perceptual environment in which various levels of attention and attunement are in play. Thibaud further remarks that ambience situates us in a "certain bodily and emotive disposition" that is experienced, meaning, importantly, that ambience cannot be reduced to interpretative acts; it is a "diffuse, disseminated presence" not reducible to the salience we customarily seek through interpretation and analysis (4). In this way, ambience is given a more vital quality; it is not an impartial medium but an ensemble of variables, forces, and elements that shape things in ways difficult to quantify or specify. These elements are simultaneously present and withdrawn, active and reactive, and complexly interactive among themselves as much as with human beings. Indeed, as Thibaud argues via J. J. Gibson, on this count human perception is not solely human doing, since it requires activity that re-

sponds to and depends on the external environs being perceived (Thibaud 8).1 address these issues more extensively in chapters 5 and 6.

Indeed, to give an example that bridges the millennia. we can compare the designed use of Lascaux as afforded by its spatial, acoustic, and material properties to musicians' attempts to get a certain sound by recording in a specific environment. For instance, some of John Bonham's most famous drum sounds on Led Zeppelin albums-reputedly the most sampled drums in the digital age-were achieved using specific recording techniques in suitable places, such as the former poorhouse Headley Grange, in East Hampshire. England. Such sound-the "sound of sound," as it were-was achieved by making the environs integral to the recording process. In songs such as Led Zeppelin IV's "When the Levee Breaks," the recording captured not just Bonham playing the drums or just the drums responding to the room but the room responding to the drums (E. Davis 74). 6 We understand that recording technology is artfully deployed to capture not an isolated drum sound or just a drum sound as perfected through Bonham's considerable technique but a sound's ambient fulfillment in an environment that brings its own unique qualities. In another environment, other qualities emerge, and even with the same drums and drummer in the same band, a different sound will result. Thus, despite the differences in technologies and purposes. in principle the ambient songs at Lascaux and Headley Grange remain the same.

Ambience and Attunement

While perception remains important to understanding ambience, other important aspects include feeling, mood, intuition, and decision making. This gets us to the issue of attunement. That is, ambience involves more than just the whole person, as it were; ambience is inseparable from the person in the environment that gives rise to ambience. There is no person who can then be tacked onto the environment. Attunement is not additive. Rather, there is a fundamental entanglement, with the individuation of particular facets being an achieved disclosure. Thus, wakefulness to ambience is not a subjective achievement but rather an ambient occurrence: an attunement. Attunement can, of course, take place at numerous levels, with consciousne ss being only one. Further, attunement is nothing static. It is always ongoing, and achievement of some sense of harmony or synchronicity would, on this account, be fleeting. It is not given that we are simply at home, in ourselves, in our lives, in our world. As I will argue more fully later on, attunement is given in its dynamic unfolding by an originary,

This, however, is precisely what renders advertising, or at least much of it, shrill. Forms of rhetoric that disclose the world and place human beings as resources for maximizing advantage, as most advertising does, eschew or foreclose the rich ecological relationality of being-in-the-world. That is, such forms deattune us. One cannot simply castigate this move. of course. One ought not simply say that advertising is wrong or evil, nor am I making any such argument. But neither should we ignore how advertising can convey narrowly suasive aspects of our being to disproportionally outsize all others, like eating nothing but cake all day. Other ambient variables that could condition advertising in its specific messages (you need cheap tacos at 2 a.m. !) or larger sayings (Consume!) are dimmed. This dimming contributes simultaneously to advertising's power and to our phenomenological reaction to it as shrill, as too sweet. A diet of advertising is unsustainable. And for this reason, while advertising is rhetoric, neither good nor ill, it would be an error to posit it as illuminating rhetoric's basic principle. Of course, this is precisely what, say, philosophy commonly does: thinly slice rhetoric as a manipulative version of persuasion, so that we see its shrillest forms as constituting its primary essence. A "sustainable" rhetoric (I discuss sustainability and sufficiency in chapters 7 and 8) is one that brings us to the richer experiences already spoken through language's saying, not solely as a sign system, but as the ch orographic background resounding of our attunement to the world.in

Heidegger's theory oflanguage allows us to rethink rhetoric as persuasion so as to take it out of a delimiting subject/object framework. Persuasion is certainly an affordance of rhetorical interaction, but an ambient perspective lets us see that taking rhetoric as persuasion narrowly and subjectively defined deflects our emplacement in the background "relation of all relations" that is language and distances us from the conditioning sway of the nonhuman that also gives place and bearing to rhetoric (Heidegger, OWL 135). Rhetoric emerges from our being-in-the-world, then, precisely also as a response to the way the world attunes and speaks us, but a response that allows for new forms of revealing that transform, at least potentially, how we are in relation to the world. This grants that even ifwe keep rhetoric always within language's orbit, language is never simply the doing of human beings, so that the wellspring of what rhetoric is and can be is opened through an attunement to its ambience. That is, rhetoric not only

receives its bearings from an attunement to all aspects of worldly existence that give rise to ways of being, human and nonhuman, but does so without mistaking any given presencing as ultimate being. Rhetoric thereby shares in a partiality that, rather than limits us, offers us hope for further and enriching unfoldings in rhetorical being.

The Rhetorical Thing

Objective, Subjective, Ambient

Only when man becomes the subject do non-human beings become objects.

-Martin Heidegger, Parmenides

"Words and things" is the entirely serious title ofa problem. -Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge

Objects themselves, far from the insipid physical bulks that one imagines, are already aflame with ambiguity, torn by vibrations and insurgencies equaling those found in the mosttortured human moods.

-Graham Harman, Tool-Being

Rhetoric has always dealt with things, which is to say that rhetoric has not ignored the material realm. The field's historically predominant focus on rhetor, audience, and language may obscure this point, but contemporary rhetorical theory in particular attends to materiality. For instance, the field has firmly incorporated Marx's notion of dialectical materialism and its attendant critique of ideology. In addition, substantial contemporary work has investigated technology, institutions, and bodies. Indeed, even the notion of materiality is increasingly thematized in its own right as worthy of direct scholarly attention (Biesecker and Lucaites, Kochin). But the problem has always been how and to what extent materiality itself matters. As a long tradition has had it, rhetoric, being one of the seven liberal arts and crucial for the formation of what we call the humanities, is most fundamentally an affair of human beings and their dealings. It is overwhelmingly discursive, a verbal art. So, yes, things matter, but as objects of concern for rhetoric or as part of the

In terms of an ambient rhetoric, we must not simply turn our sights to sound and ask how we can now use sound to generate desired affective responses. As I stated earlier, we need more than a sonic semiotic. That would certainly be a possibility, but it obscures the deeper insights that sonics thought ambiently can afford us. We can do more with this insight into the ambience of design than single out and focus on various strands, such as the functional (how usable it is), the cognitive (what it means for us), or the affective (how it makes us feel). Instead, we could build a fresh, cumulative list of things with which we might concern ourselves as teachers, writers, and rhetoricians. I have argued that it is better to see them as complexly generating an overarching ambient environment that cradles, without forcing, particular affective responses or that fosters an attunement (as with "clear, confident, and connected," which is Microsoft's take on a positive, secure feeling that will enable work and play). Such a perspective reflects a fuller, less instrumental view of human beings and their interactions, particularly multimedia rhetorics. It deprivileges dir ectly conscious experience and boosts the importance of indirect, unconscious, auratic, osmotic, and ambient phenomena. Put differently, such rhet orical design

organizes an experience, not so much to persuade in any direct sense, but to attune and inflect our sense of bodily inhabitance and the cradle of intelligibility within which we comport ourselves. It is worth recalling Eno's irony-laden dismissal of the corporate sloganeering Microsoft delivered to him as part of the project. If Microsoft perhaps intended more direct forms of marketing and the shaping of the user's experience, including the service of avant-garde musicians to brand Microsoft products, it is important that Eno's music resists such narrowing. For Eno, ambient music is inherently political, evoking new senses of place and how human beings inhabit it; this includes, more pointedly, a reduced role for human agency reflecting a more distributed, ecological approach to will, action, and consequence. The lengthy video session with Robert Fripp and the Microsoft team suggests that such aesthetics and their politics, however indirect, are nevertheless in play. So, while startup music itself makes up only a small element amid these far larger concerns (not to mention the larger expanse of sonic space and its rhetorical-architectural possibilities), possibly one of little relevance, it nevertheless can open us onto a deeper reflection concerning our relation to technology, space, and sonics, and we lose much ifwe ignore the insights it grants.

Because the Timaeus deals pervasively with the question of beginnings, it is appropriate to see it also as a recommencement of the task that was central to the Republic, which is to bring Athens back to its ideal form (at the time of the dialogue, apparently, the interlocutors saw it as less than it had been). What we learn from the Republic is that while the ideal city they describe evokes powerful feelings and approval, it remains an ideal. It misses actuality, and the discussants hope this condition is rectifiable, that this city ideal can be brought to life and seen vigorously exercising as states do (Timaeus 18b). As it is, the ideal city is a dead city. Sallis remarks that, strictly speaking, it is a "technical city," a city of the head achieved through philosophical technique (20). Not only is it a fabricated artifact of thought, but it lacks eros, which is to say, it lacks becoming in a generative sense. The fact that the Republic focuses strongly on controlling eros and all that goes with it, such as "procreation, mating, birth, sexual difference, [and] corporeity itself in its singularity," takes on greater significance in this context (Sallis 26). There is thus a tension between control as something intellectual and life as something that exceeds the intellectual. For this reason, among others, Sallis tells us that from the very beginning, the Timaeus comments on the limits of fabrication, whether as techne or poiesis, with respect to eros (26). This is very much a problem of invention in the sense of finding ways to actualize or enact what are initially only ideas, feelings, or intuitions. That is, the Platonic chora addresses the question of the available means of creation and how we give life to and make a place for (static) ideas. Furthermore, the discussion implicitly evokes a distinction

between the made and the born, or between techni and physis. The chora gains even greater import when we see that it emerges precisely to dissolve such distinctions and give life to artifice.

Friedrich Solmsen argues that we can understand Plato to be wrestling with a problem that reaches far back into debates carried on by the pre-Socratics. How is one to understand genesis, or becoming? Parmenides is held to have dismissed any outright genesis; Empedocles refined Parmenides's thought, suggesting instead that something akin t omixture, achieved through the interactions of the four elements or roots (see chapter 7), could replace genesis. The Timaeus itself addresses this issue, but it does so as a reopening of the question of becoming. Throughout the dialogue, the uncertainty of knowing anything about genesis is remarked, and even the accounts given are characterized as only probable or likely (Timaeus 28b, 44d, 48c-d, 55d, 59c. 66d). ln this regard, the ch6ra can be taken as Plato's attempt to reintroduce the notion of becoming, even ifhe steps back from the more assertive positions of his predecessors (Solmsen 40). At the risk of oversimplifying, we might say that Plato posited this refined notion of genesis as an aid in thinking through how, as Algra puts it, the sensible world participates in the intelligible world (3). Ann Ashbaugh makes a similar point when she claims that the Timaeus was the mast important Platonic dialogue in antiquity because it addressed a fundamental question, one that we have yet to answer definitively: not "what an objective cosmos is, but how it comes to be known by the souln (1). Apropos ofSallis's comment on the limits of fabrication, the Republic already carries in germinal form this very question: haw does one move from ideas, or the realm of the Forms. to the sensible, active world?

This sensible, active world is not one of simple presence or mundane materiality. The Greeks, like other ancient peoples, had a strong sense of what remains hidden, obscure, and withdrawn in the world. Indeed. the ancient sense of the divine was itself tethered to place, as E. V. Walter argues throughout his book Placeways. Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

So far I have been arguing that dwelling and the fourfold grant insight into an originary affectability materialized in things and in the world's worlding. Heidegger, of course, would not put it this way (i.e., in t erms of affectability), but we ought not simply transmute affectability into determinism or authoritative demand, as if we could short-circuit dwelling with others in the world into a philosophical version of a command-control

In short, like everything else, dwelling resists any reduction to forms of simple presence, in this case, to directly available and revealed best practices for homemaking. If we were always already at home, if home were never at issue (never a "thing" for us), then homemaking would not be challenging for us; ultimately it can never be fully realized. Dwelling is an ongoing and never stilled process ofattunement, disclosure, and building. Thus, dwelling is rhetorical in an ambient sense: disclosure and attunement emerge out of a worldly affectability, so that dwelling's coming to manifestation is a matter of ongoing differentiation. In what follows, I will try to elaborate on this point more plainly; specifically, I will try to rethink stability in an ambient key, arguing that it is less a cessation of movement or change than a way of dwelling attuned to sustainability and achieved through the lived realization of sufficiency.

Dwelling in/as Sufficiency

Bringing Heidegger's concept of dwelling into ongoing struggles with sustainability, particularly regarding the automobile, does not just show but performs how humans become cognizant of and organize their practices around what in contemporary environmental discourse we would call an ecology, or things and forces joined together in dynamic coexistence sustainable over time. The English word ecology, which derives from the German Okologie, coined by the biologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866, stems from the ancient Greek word oikos, meaning "house," "home," or "dwelling." Haeckel drew on oikos to bring home the sense of ecology as a comprehensive science of an organism's relation to its environment,

with environment here being where one dwells (Thiele.Indra's 3). As I have shown, when Heidegger discusses dwelling, he describes the relation not only as one of directly co-responding but as one of hearkening to directives or being conditioned by things; for Heidegger, that is, ecology entails more than presence. Ecological literature, however, often describes ecologies in (sometimes overly) holistic terms focused on the powerful role of the feedback loops that emerge within circulating, sustaining activities and material interactions. Feedback loops supply necessary encouragement and constraint allowing for the dynamic self-organization characteristic of a flourishing ecology; this can even be attributed to a direct sense of a "natural" law that we must acknowledge or follow.• Regulatory mechanisms and their "values" are in a sense "built in" to an ecological system. Thus ecologies are often characterized in terms of efficiency, since they tend to reward the maximization of potential. At the same time. ecologies curtail or otherwise redirect efficiency so that nothing gets too far out of balance; if it does, the ecology "self-corrects," adapts, morphs, or fails in accordance with autopoesis, or self-organization (Maturana and Varela, 47-52; Varela, Thompson, and Rosch 88-91: Hayles 136). In short, while efficiency certainly constitutes a vector for an ecology, the notion relevant here can significantly differ from the kind of abstracted and totalized notion of efficiency common to instrumentalized technological thinking,5Efficiency matters because an ecology is at every moment entangled in constraining forces-checks and balances, if you will-necessary for a sustainable trajectory. Insofar as efficiency is thus always tempered, we might better consider it an example of sufficiency. In a sustainable ecological system, efficiency emerges as forms of sufficiency (Thiele, Timely 179).

What is at stake in this qualification of efficiency? We might keep in mind the general definition of efficiency: maximum yield for minimum effort, a point that resonates with Heidegger's arguments about technological enframing insofar as both can be conceived as forms of ordering (QCT 8, 15)_ More precisely, technology already conditions how efficiency is conceived and I ived. This occurs not deterministically but rather ontologically. in shaping how worldly affordances reveal themselves as what they are, for technology is a way of revealing the world, or more pointedly, a revealing that challenges (herausfordern) the world as a standing reserve (Bestand), a stockpile of resources to be exploited (QCT 17). I explored this idea in previous chapters through discussions of Sputnik andEarthrise. As a rhetorician, however, I am suspicious of the separation of form and content that structures this narrative: Windows is a transparent, functional entity allowing us to conduct our business (even if our business is pleasure), and the startup music is the flourish, the rhetorical ornament dressing up Windows's transparent instrumentality. And basically the same narrative is often used to dismiss rhetoric, which is too often seen as the decorative frill dressing up language to make it more pleasing, persuasive. or seductive but in the end unimportant and even pernicious because it impedes the facts we can transparently represent in communicative linguistic utility. This narrative dates back at least to Plato, who used it to trump rhetoric with philosophy, and it rouses my suspicions if it is applied to understanding why Windows has startup music. Something else is at stake. More precisely, I am going to argue that examining something as small as an operating system's startup music can open a window on understanding our relation to computers and computer software. Microsoft Windows and similar entities are not just operating systems or software we use; rather, they constitute an actual environment, and in so doing, they require an extension of our modes of comportment to include more com-

plete reflections of the human. A functionalist view of Windows that casts its startup music as frippery does more than replicate age-old arguments against rhetoric; it implicitly reduces our understanding of the richness of human being. As I will show, this view conflicts with the apparent goals of the Windows designers themselves. We might go a step further and acknowledge that startup music helps create a more complete package, one with more emotional pull than mere functionality provides. This gets us on the right track, I think, but it is the kind of statement that invites deeper reflection. That is, asserting that music affects us begs the question of how it in fact does so. Here, then, I address how a musical snippet involves and inflects a user-how, that is, it helps environ a situation in which various modalities of suasion become possible.

Ultimately I will conclude that an ambient rhetoric opens rhetorical study to music differently than previous accounts have allowed. As I have argued elsewhere, music evokes three dominant responses.1 The oldest argument, one repeated by Plato and Aristotle, is that it affects us emotionally, and while such a response can be a boon, it should also rouse our suspicions and our guard, since it opens us to personal and cultural decadence. Hence, music must be properly modulated and controlled. The second argument is that its indeterminacy and lack of semantic content make music a limited art; determinate symbolic arts are superior and preferable. The third, which I have already mentioned, is that music is ornamental to human life but not essential. The distrust characterizing these positions should spark us. There is something amiss when music evokes such paradoxical positions, described simultaneously as powerful, indeterminate, and inessential. Further, beyond the inherent contradictions, these positions seem tainted by various modalities of suspicion that resonate with the ire rhetoric too has continually inspired through the millennia. And if the first argument has its kernel of truth, if, that is, music does affect us deeply, then we must see that music involves rhetoric. In this chapter I will attempt to theorize this relation in an ambient modality.

Given that an ambient rhetoric is attuned to the material environment, it would be unfitting to examine music in isolation. Hence, a secondary argument in this chapter will serve to puzzle out some of the deeper, richer relations we want with our technologies and how such understanding reconfigures the grounding assumptions we bring to studies of interactive media. This matters for a number ofreasons.
